newsitem.title: SPAIN: Purported proof of Spain's "dirty war" published.
newsitem.headline: Purported proof of Spain's "dirty war" published.

text.p: A Spanish newspaper published leaked government papers on Monday purporting to prove the former Socialist administration set up death squads which waged a "dirty war" against ETA Basque separatist rebels in the 1980s.
Attorney General Juan Ortiz Urculo said the documents could provide evidence for reopening a high-level investigation of former government officials.
"We have to verify if they are authentic and if they are considered classified," he told state radio. "Each case has to be studied and re-weighed, but the road is open."

The Anti-Terrorist Liberation Groups (GAL) killed 28 people in 1983-87. Allegations that they were set up and funded by the state contributed to the election defeat last March of former prime minister Felipe Gonzalez's socialist government.

Supreme Court judges investigating the "dirty war" voted six to four last month against questioning Gonzalez, who denies involvement, but left the way open to reverse the decision if new evidence emerged.

The papers published in the pro-conservative El Mundo purport to show directly that Spain's military intelligence agency CESID set up GAL and also selected the first victim: alleged ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom) rebel Ramon Onederra.
Onederra was gunned down in a bar in the Basque region of southwestern France in December 1983, one month after his name appeared on the list of prime GAL targets quoted by El Mundo.
The defence ministry said on Monday it was "radically false" that there was any sort of document in which CESID picked out GAL targets.
"It appears to be a partial transcript of a certain court paper more than any sort of investigation," the statement said.
The courts are seeking the declassification of some 20 spy documents that supposedly give details of the GAL campaign of bombings, kidnap, torture and murder.
Senior officials, including former interior minister Jose Barrionuevo, have been charged in the "dirty war" case, but courts have been stymied by a lack of solid evidence.
El Mundo said it would publish all the supposedly secret documents in a series that it started on Monday.

The government has refused to hand over the papers, citing reasons of state security. But the Supreme Court is studying the case and is expected to make a ruling early next year on whether or not the government can be forced to comply.
Ortiz Urculo said he had recommended declassification in another case when secret papers turned up in public.
Gonzalez, in remarks to reporters, said he was "absolutely unconcerned" about the publication of the papers.
"This affair is apparently being debated in the Supreme Court," he said. "I have the highest respect for any decision it should take."
But the leftwing opposition group United Left (IU) said the papers confirmed that the evidence to convict former government officials existed and it called for a full investigation.

"It confirms the evidence of documentation fundamental for definitively clearing up the GAL case," IU spokesman Willy Meyer said. "It's imperative that Parliament investigate the dirty war against ETA as long as there are people involved in this affair still seated in positions of political responsibility."
